title: Thailand seeks lower tariffs after breakthrough in US trade talks
text:
Thailand seeks lower tariffs after breakthrough in US trade talks | Lianhe Zaobao 
 Singapore International China Business Opinion Lifestyle Entertainment Search Published / 18 Nov 2026 20:56 S M L XL Thailand seeks lower tariffs after breakthrough in US trade talks
 AI-translated article with transliterated names. Read original Chinese article here. 
 Thailand Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul (left) and US President Donald Trump signed a joint statement on the Thailand-US Agreement on Reciprocal Trade on Tuesday (17 November), while attending the 49th ASEAN Summit and related meetings in the Philippines. The statement confirmed that both sides had reached agreement on the core elements of the trade negotiations. （AFP） (Bangkok, agencies) Thailand and the US have reached agreement on the core terms of a reciprocal trade agreement, with the text expected to be finalised within two months. 
 Thailand Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and US President Donald Trump signed a joint statement on the Thailand-US Agreement on Reciprocal Trade on Tuesday (17 November), while attending the 49th ASEAN Summit and related meetings in the Philippines. The statement confirmed that both sides had reached agreement on the core elements of the trade negotiations. 
 Deputy Prime Minister and Commerce Minister Suphajee Suthumpun said on Wednesday (18 November) that Thailand would seek a reduction in the US tariff rate on goods linked to forced labour under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, from the current 12.5% to 10%. This would bring the rate into line with those for regional competitors such as Malaysia, Indonesia and Cambodia, helping Thai exports remain competitive. 
 Thailand’s The Nation reported that Suphajee said Thailand was also seeking assurances from the US that overall tariffs on Thai products would not exceed 19%. However, Thailand would closely monitor possible US tariff measures under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act and Section 122 of the Trade Act. 
 She also said the two sides’ legal teams were expected to need about two months to finalise the agreement’s text. However, the agreement must still go through approval procedures, including Thai cabinet approval, public consultation and parliamentary scrutiny. With the US year-end holiday season also approaching, it was unlikely to be signed this year and could take several months to come into effect. 
 Suphajee also clarified that Thailand had not agreed to eliminate tariffs on all US imports, as Trump had said. She said Thailand would not immediately open its market fully or implement 100% trade liberalisation, in order to protect sensitive domestic industries. 
 Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on US exports and "remove substantial non-tariff barriers on American vehicles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, ethanol, and poultry," Trump said at a press conference on Tuesday while attending the ASEAN leaders’ summit. 
 He said Thailand would also buy an additional US$2.6 billion (about S$3.354 billion) worth of US agricultural products. "This is an incredible victory for both countries." 
 The US is Thailand’s largest export market. Thai exports to the US totalled about 2.37 trillion baht (about S$90.5 billion) last year. 
 Separately, Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow warned that the latest US restrictions on the export and use of high-end semiconductors could affect Thailand’s plans to become a regional data centre hub. 
 The Bureau of Industry and Security, which comes under the US Department of Commerce, announced new rules on Monday (16 November) tightening controls on advanced semiconductor exports. These include designating Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil as higher-risk transshipment countries. 
 In an interview with Bloomberg Television on Wednesday, Sihasak said most of the affected countries were US friends and partners, and that Thailand would need to consult Washington on how to respond. 
 Asked whether the US was using chips as leverage in trade negotiations, Sihasak said, “we try not to look at it that way”. 
 He added that the controls were not aimed at Thailand or neighbouring countries, but were intended to prevent the chips from reaching China. 
 Suphajee said the advanced chips covered by the new restrictions accounted for only about 0.7% of the total value of Thailand’s chip imports, and no widespread impact was currently expected.
